Consult Summary:  
45-year-old physically active female marathon trainee presents with a two-week history of right knee pain and intermittent clicking aggravated by running and gym exercises, likely representing an overuse injury with possible meniscal irritation; mild prior trauma and transient toe tingling noted.

History:  
- Presenting complaint: Right knee pain with clicking for approximately two weeks, aggravated by running (notably after 2.5-3 miles) and gym exercises involving knee flexion and extension (abs work). Mild swelling noted initially which resolved with ice. Occasional right toe tingling after running, one episode. Mild pitting edema in legs noticed after prolonged standing (sock indentations), no persistent swelling. No locking, giving way, or instability of the knee reported.  
- Timeline: Symptoms began around two weeks ago after increased running mileage in marathon training starting about one month ago. Pain starts roughly after 20 minutes or 2.5-3 miles of running. Patient has reduced long runs recently due to worsening pain. Swelling initially present post-run, resolved with ice. Clicking noted intermittently especially with leg flexion/extension movements during exercise.  
- Exacerbating factors: Running, particularly beyond 2.5 miles; gym exercises involving knee flexion/extension (abs workouts).  
- Relieving factors: Ice application reduces swelling and discomfort; pain absent at rest and sitting; occasional NSAIDs (Ibuprofen) provide symptomatic relief.  
- Associated symptoms: Occasional tingling in right toes post-run (single episode); mild intermittent leg edema after standing; no joint instability, locking, or giving way; no redness, warmth, or systemic symptoms. No back pain or involvement of other joints.  
- Systems review: No gastrointestinal, respiratory, or systemic symptoms reported; no fever, no persistent swelling or skin changes in legs; no neurological deficits aside from isolated tingling episode.

Past Medical History:  
- Far-sightedness with LASIK surgery.  
- Past urinary tract infection with suspected kidney stones requiring ER evaluation, no chronic kidney disease.  
- Occasional joint issues previously, not frequent or severe.  
- No chronic musculoskeletal or autoimmune disorders noted.  
- Medications: Occasional Ibuprofen (max 400 mg), Vitamin D supplement, Melatonin (for sleep), Aleve (dose/route/frequency not documented), occasional Xanax (dose/route/frequency not documented). Marijuana use noted.  
- No drug allergies mentioned.

Social History:  
- Physically active, training for marathon (started increased running about one month ago).  
- Plays sports including ice hockey; sustained minor ice hockey injury (bruise) a few months ago.  
- Occasional recreational marijuana use.  
- No mention of smoking tobacco or alcohol consumption.  
- Lives at home in London; no financial or lifestyle concerns discussed.

Family History:  
- Not documented in transcript.

Physical Examination:  
- Not documented except for verbal report from patient indicating:  
  - No current swelling or tenderness at rest.  
  - Full range of motion (full flexion and extension).  
  - No locking or instability of the right knee.  
  - No redness, heat, or deformity.  
  - Mild pitting edema noted after prolonged standing (patient-reported).  
- Vitals not documented.

Investigations:  
- None performed or reported.  
- No imaging or labs ordered or available.

Assessment & Plan:

Issue 1: Right knee pain and clicking likely due to overuse injury with possible meniscal irritation or patellofemoral syndrome.  
- Assessment: Pain onset coinciding with recent increase in running mileage; symptoms aggravated by running and knee flexion/extension; intermittent clicking; no mechanical locking or instability. History of minor trauma possibly contributory.  
- Plan:  
  - Continue ice therapy as effective first-line management.  
  - Advise reducing or modifying running intensity/distance to avoid exacerbation.  
  - Recommend physiotherapy referral for detailed knee assessment and guided rehabilitation.  
  - Prescribe stronger anti-inflammatory medication as alternative to Ibuprofen (dose/route/frequency per prescribing physician).  
  - Educate patient to monitor for concerning signs (persistent swelling, heat, redness, inability to move knee, systemic symptoms) requiring urgent medical review.  
  - Consider further imaging if symptoms persist post-physiotherapy assessment.

Issue 2: Occasional tingling in right toes post-run, possibly mild nerve irritation or neuropathy.  
- Assessment: Single transient episode without persistent neurological deficits or systemic causes identified.  
- Plan:  
  - Monitor for recurrence or progression of neurological symptoms.  
  - Address underlying knee pathology to reduce mechanical irritation.  
  - No immediate investigations indicated unless symptoms worsen.

Issue 3: Mild intermittent lower leg edema consistent with possible venous insufficiency or dependent edema.  
- Assessment: Patient reports sock indentations after standing without redness, warmth, pain, or other vascular signs; no clinical suspicion of DVT.  
- Plan:  
  - Advise leg elevation when possible.  
  - Encourage regular movement and avoid prolonged standing.  
  - Monitor for changes such as persistent swelling, pain, or redness which would warrant further vascular evaluation.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):  
- Overuse Injury with possible Meniscal Irritation or Patellofemoral Syndrome (High likelihood): Supported by recent increase in running, localized pain and clicking, and prior minor trauma; symptoms start after several miles, no locking or instability.  
- Mild Knee Inflammation or Synovitis (Moderate likelihood): Initial mild swelling responsive to ice and NSAIDs; no systemic signs; likely reactive to overuse or minor injury.  
- Mild Peripheral Neuropathy or Nerve Irritation (Low to Moderate likelihood): Single episode of toe tingling post-run potentially from mechanical nerve irritation; no permanent neurological deficit or underlying metabolic cause identified.  
- Venous Insufficiency or Mild Peripheral Edema (Low likelihood): Sock indentations noted; no inflammatory vascular signs; unlikely to account for knee symptoms.  
- Ligamentous Injury (Low to Moderate likelihood): Prior ice hockey trauma could predispose; absence of instability or giving way decreases probability.

Quality checks:  
- Allergies not documented; clarification recommended.  
- Medication doses and frequencies for Aleve, Melatonin, Xanax not fully documented.  
- No physical exam by clinician available in transcript; examination findings rely on patient report.  
- No imaging or laboratory investigations performed; may be necessary depending on symptom evolution.  
- No family history documented; consider inquiry in follow-up.  
- No conflicts between transcript and DDx; DDx supports clinical impression and management.  
- Transcript audio quality sufficient for accurate extraction.
